title: Vana: exile
hook: in the forest, Draupadi argues for anger and Yudhishthira argues for forgiveness, and the epic lets them both speak
carry: a time for strength, or to let go

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna came to the Vana, the forest, and Draupadi told him everything. Your line was let them finish before you answer. Did you let someone finish before you answered? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

An evening in the forest, and a married couple is having a real argument. Draupadi looks at her husband in his bark clothes, sleeping on the ground, and she can't stand it. You were a king, she says. Your brothers are suffering. How is your anger not blazing? Yudhishthira doesn't storm out. He answers her, at length. And she answers back. The epic doesn't cut this scene short or tell us who won. It gives both of them the floor. Today, the great forest argument: anger or forgiveness?
screen: `A COUPLE ARGUES IN THE FOREST.` → `WHY IS YOUR ANGER NOT BLAZING?` → `BOTH OF THEM GET THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't argue from feeling alone. She brings a story. Long ago, she says, the demon king Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada, the same Prahlada whose verdict Vidura told in the hall, a question: which is better, forgiveness or might? And Prahlada answered: neither one, always. Someone who forgives everything is treated with contempt, even by his own servants. Someone who never forgives makes enemies of everyone. There's a time for each, and wisdom is knowing which time it is. Now, says Draupadi, is the time for might. Yudhishthira answers with a different picture. Anger, he says, is the root of destruction. An angry person can't tell what should be said from what shouldn't, and will harm even those who deserve no harm. Forgiveness, in his telling, is what holds the world together; if there were no one who forgave, there would be no peace among people at all. He calls forgiveness the strength of the strong. So who is right? This is what makes the scene worth sitting with. Draupadi isn't the hothead and Yudhishthira isn't the saint. Both of them quote the wisdom of their tradition. Both of them are suffering. Draupadi's point is about timing: forgiveness offered always can become weakness. Yudhishthira's point is about the self: anger acted on can burn the one who carries it. And the forest is where they can say all this. There's no court here, no audience of kings. Just two people who lost the same things, disagreeing honestly about what to do next.
screen: `PRAHLADA: A TIME FOR EACH.` · `DRAUPADI: NOW IS THE TIME FOR MIGHT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: ANGER DESTROYS.` · then, large: `BOTH QUOTE THEIR TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and feel your feet or your seat. Bring to mind one thing that still makes you angry. Not the biggest; a medium one will do. Breathe in, and let Draupadi's question rise: is this a time for strength? Breathe out, and let Yudhishthira's rise: what would this anger do to me if I carried it? You don't need to settle the argument. Just let both voices speak while you breathe. If you pray, you can bring that situation into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for forgiveness, and both are heard.
Your line: a time for strength, or to let go. Today, before you act on anger, ask the question Prahlada answered: is this a time for strength, or a time to let go? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Teachers and commentators return to this forest debate between Draupadi and Yudhishthira when discussing anger, forgiveness and right action, and Prahlada's answer to Bali is retold on its own as well.

match.prompt: the forest argument — tap the pairs.
pairs: now is the time for might
anger is the root of destruction

myth: Prahlada said forgiveness is always best
he said neither forgiveness nor might is right every time; wisdom knows which time it is.
Draupadi supported her argument with an old story
she told of Bali asking his grandfather Prahlada about forgiveness and might.
the epic declares Draupadi wrong and moves on
it gives both speakers long answers and lets the argument stand.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Draupadi says it's time for might, and she has a wise old story to back her up. what do you answer?
options: agree and march on Hastinapura tonight.
answer that anger destroys, and forgiveness holds the world together.
fork.reveal: he answers at length, calling anger the root of destruction and forgiveness what keeps peace among people. and Draupadi answers him back.

trapdoor: what you thought: Draupadi is angry and Yudhishthira is calm, end of story.
what it means: both argue from their tradition's wisdom; she stresses timing, he stresses what anger does to the angry.
what a scholar hears: an old story set inside the argument, Prahlada and Bali, gives Draupadi's case its own authority.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the dialogue of Draupadi and Yudhishthira in the forest (Draupadi's reproach; the conversation of Prahlada and Bali; Yudhishthira on anger and forgiveness)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli that Draupadi tells the Prahlada and Bali (Vali) conversation, and the gist of Prahlada's answer (neither always forgiveness nor always might; contempt for the always-forgiving).
Confirm Yudhishthira's points: anger as the root of destruction; the angry cannot tell what should be said; forgiveness keeps peace among creatures; 'the might of the mighty' or similar.
Ganguli's text includes verses attributed to Kashyapa praising forgiveness; left out because exact wording isn't certain.
The later part of the debate (Draupadi on why the good suffer, Yudhishthira on acting without seeking reward) is left for another day or for a Keeper's choice.

Editor: day 774 told Vidura's story of Prahlada judging against his son Virochana; added a clause tying this Prahlada (Virochana's father, Bali's grandfather) to that one, so listeners don't hear a repeat or a different figure. Confirm the identification in Ganguli.
Audit: the carry called it 'Prahlada's question', but the question was Bali's and Prahlada gave the answer; reworded to 'the question Prahlada answered'.
